Codespaces runs the repository on a machine in the cloud, from your browser. It is free within a monthly allowance that a session with the script barely touches. Every scenario works there, and it is the simplest way to test webhooks.

  1. Fork the repository to your account: github.com/mguyard/pydiagral/fork. Untick Copy the main branch only, so that your fork also gets beta, the branch with the latest version of pydiagral and of this script. Later, the Sync fork button of your fork brings it up to date.

  2. Create the codespace with New with options: on your fork, Code > Codespaces, then the ⋯ menu > New with options.

    1. Pick the beta branch.

    2. The page asks for the secrets the dev container suggests, the variables of Configure. GitHub shows none as mandatory, since it lets you leave any empty, but the script needs:

      • DIAGRAL_USERNAME and DIAGRAL_PASSWORD: always;
      • DIAGRAL_SERIAL_ID: for every scenario but ping and systems. If you do not know it, leave it empty, run systems to find it, then add it as described in the note below;
      • DIAGRAL_PIN_CODE: to read the status and details, and to arm or disarm.

      This page saves the values you enter in your account's Codespaces secrets. So when you create another codespace, a secret entered the first time shows Associated with repository instead of a field: the codespace uses the saved value. Change it as described in the note below.

    3. Click Create codespace. It starts the repository's dev container, with pydiagral and every tool installed. On first start, it opens this guide in a browser tab; its terminal shows the guide's address on every start.

    GitHub keeps these secrets encrypted in your account, never in the repository, and gives them to the script as environment variables. It does not ask again for your next codespaces on this fork.

  3. Run the commands of Run in the codespace's terminal, with:

    • python try_pydiagral.py … to try the code of the branch the codespace opened;
    • uv run try_pydiagral.py … to try the latest release, betas included.

Adding or changing a secret afterwards

Only New with options asks for the secrets. If you created the codespace with the Create codespace on … button instead, or left a secret empty, add it yourself:

  1. open Settings > Codespaces on GitHub, and click New secret;
  2. enter its name, DIAGRAL_SERIAL_ID for instance, and its value;
  3. under Repository access, select your fork.

To change a value, edit the secret on the same page.

In both cases, stop and restart the codespace (Codespaces: Stop Current Codespace in the command palette, or from github.com/codespaces): a codespace reads its secrets when it starts.

Stop the codespace once done, and delete it when you no longer need it: its storage counts against the allowance as long as it exists.

docs.title: On your machine
docs.text:
Download try_pydiagral.py and .env.example into the same folder, or clone the repository.

The recommended way to run the script is uv. The script declares what it needs at its top (inline script metadata), and uv run installs it in an environment of its own, apart from your other projects: nothing else to install.

Always the latest pydiagral

The script is meant to show what the library does today: on every run, uv checks for the latest pydiagral, betas included, and uses it. A new release can take a few minutes to show up, while uv's cache of the package index expires.

Without uv, install the dependencies yourself, ideally in a virtual environment, and run the commands below with python instead of uv run:

pip install --upgrade --pre pydiagral python-dotenv

--pre lets pip pick a beta. Run the same command again to move to a newer release.

Testing your own changes to pydiagral

uv run always takes pydiagral from PyPI, even inside the repository. To try a local change, install the repository in editable mode (PYPROJECT_VERSION=0.1.0-dev pip install -e ".[dev]", which the dev container does for you) and run python try_pydiagral.py.

docs.title: 2. Configure
docs.text:
Where the settings come from depends on where the script runs:

  • In Codespaces, the secrets you entered on New with options are the settings: nothing to do here. To add an optional one from the table below, or one you left empty, see the note Adding or changing a secret afterwards above.
  • On your machine, copy .env.example to .env, next to the script, and fill it in.

Every variable starts with DIAGRAL_, and an empty value counts as unset:

Variable Needed for Purpose DIAGRAL_USERNAME everything The e-mail address of your Diagral account DIAGRAL_PASSWORD everything The password of your Diagral account DIAGRAL_SERIAL_ID every scenario but ping and systems The serial ID of your box. Run the systems scenario to find it DIAGRAL_PIN_CODE status, details, and every scenario that arms Your alarm PIN code, also named master code DIAGRAL_API_KEY, DIAGRAL_SECRET_KEY optional An existing API key. Left empty, the script creates a temporary one — see API keys DIAGRAL_VENDOR optional The brand of your account: DIAGRAL (default), DAITEM, EDAITEM, LOGISTYALMA or DISTRIBUTION

Variables already set in the environment, Codespaces secrets included, take precedence over .env.

Danger

.env holds your credentials: never commit it, attach it to an issue or share it.

docs.title: 3. Run
docs.text:
The commands start with python or uv run, depending on where the script runs and which pydiagral it should use:

Where Command pydiagral used Codespaces python try_pydiagral.py … The code of the branch the codespace opened, beta of your fork: the usual choice Codespaces uv run try_pydiagral.py … The latest release on PyPI, betas included, whatever the branch Your machine, with uv uv run try_pydiagral.py … The latest release on PyPI, betas included Your machine, without uv python try_pydiagral.py … The one you installed with pip

The examples below use python; replace it with uv run where the table says so.

python try_pydiagral.py                  # every read-only scenario
python try_pydiagral.py ping systems     # only these, in this order
python try_pydiagral.py arm --wait 10    # arm, wait 10 s, then disarm
python try_pydiagral.py --help           # every scenario and option

Without arguments, the script runs every read-only scenario: nothing changes on your alarm. Each scenario prints a == name == header, what it found, then how long it took, such as (status: 2.4 s). When one fails, its error is printed with the time it took, and the next one runs.

A good first run is ping systems: it only needs the username and password, checks that the Diagral cloud answers, and shows the serial ID of each system of your account.

docs.title: Read-only — run by default
docs.text: Scenario What it shows ping Whether the Diagral cloud answers. Needs no API key systems The serial ID of each system of your account, and how many API keys each has. Needs no serial ID configuration The alarm name, its groups, and how many devices of each type it has devices Every device of the alarm, by type, with its index and label details The box model, firmware version and mode. Needs the PIN code status Whether the alarm is armed, and which groups are active. Needs the PIN code anomalies The current anomalies, by device webhook The webhook subscription, if any, with the host of its URL only automatisms The automatism rules. This call is untested: pydiagral logs a warning

docs.title: Named only — never run by default
docs.text:
Scenario What it does connection Tests the connection the way hass-diagral's setup does. Without an API key, it creates a temporary one and deletes it arm Arms the whole alarm, waits, then disarms presence Arms in presence mode, waits, then disarms partial Runs partial start 1 or 2 (--partial), waits, then disarms groups Arms the groups given by --groups, waits, then disarms webhook-listen Receives the alarm's notifications on a temporary listener — see Testing webhooks

The scenarios that arm always disarm at the end: after the wait, and when the arming call fails. If disarming itself fails, the script says so: check your alarm.

Ctrl+C depends on when you press it:

  • while the script waits or listens, as its message says, it ends that wait only: the scenarios that armed disarm at once, and the run goes on to the end, diagnostics report included;
  • at any other moment, it stops the run, after the usual clean-up: disarming, deleting the temporary API key and the webhook subscription.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Effect --wait SECONDS 30 How long the arming scenarios stay armed before disarming --timeout SECONDS 30 How long each request to Diagral may take before it fails — see Troubleshooting --partial {1,2} 1 Which partial start partial runs --groups N [N ...] 1 Which groups groups arms, e.g. --groups 1 2 --keep-apikey off Keeps the API key the script creates, and prints it --trigger {none,presence,arm} none What webhook-listen does to provoke a notification --listen-for SECONDS 120 How long webhook-listen listens --port PORT 8080 The local port webhook-listen listens on --public-url URL found alone in Codespaces The public URL of your tunnel to that port --debug off Logs every request and answer — see Debug log

docs.title: Testing webhooks
docs.text:
Diagral can push the alarm's events to a URL: state changes, alerts and anomalies. webhook-listen checks that they reach you and that pydiagral reads them. It starts a temporary listener, makes sure the public URL reaches it, subscribes it, waits for notifications and shows each one, then deletes the subscription.

One subscription per box

Diagral keeps a single webhook subscription per box. When one exists, hass-diagral's for instance, the scenario stops before doing anything, since it would replace it. With hass-diagral, disable the Diagral entry in Home Assistant (Settings > Devices & services), run the test, then enable the entry again: the integration subscribes again when the entry starts.

Diagral must reach the listener from the Internet, which a computer at home usually does not allow. Two free ways around it:

docs.title: In GitHub Codespaces — recommended
docs.text:
In a codespace set up as above, run:

python try_pydiagral.py webhook-listen

While it listens, two minutes by default, arm or disarm the alarm yourself, from a keypad, a badge or the Diagral app, and watch the notifications arrive. To let the script arm and disarm instead, see Triggers.

Nothing else is needed: the script builds the public URL of the codespace's port, makes the port public with the GitHub CLI, and makes it private again at the end. When it cannot, it says so and waits up to two minutes: in the Ports tab, right-click port 8080, then Port Visibility > Public.

docs.title: On your machine, with a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel
docs.text:
A Quick Tunnel gives a public trycloudflare.com address to a local port, without a Cloudflare account.

  1. Install cloudflared by following Cloudflare's downloads page.

  2. In another terminal, start the tunnel to the listener's port, and copy the https://….trycloudflare.com address it prints:

    bash cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080

  3. Run the scenario with that address:

    bash uv run try_pydiagral.py webhook-listen --public-url https://….trycloudflare.com

The address changes every time the tunnel starts: pass the new one on each run. Do not add --allowed-mail to the tunnel, since Diagral cannot sign in. Any other tunnel to the same port, ngrok for instance, works the same way.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
--trigger What happens none (default) The script listens for --listen-for seconds, while you arm or disarm the alarm yourself, from a keypad, a badge or the Diagral app presence The script arms in presence mode, listens for --listen-for seconds, disarms, then listens 30 seconds more for the disarm notification. Presence mode has no exit delay: the quickest way to let the script provoke a notification arm The same with the whole alarm. Its notification only arrives once the exit delay is over, about four minutes, so the script stays armed and listens at least five minutes

With presence or arm, the scenario fails when no notification arrived.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: Each notification prints its type, code and description, the group, the device type and the type of user who acted. The transmitter ID, which is your serial number, and the user name are never printed. The structure of each notification, without its values, joins the diagnostics report under webhook_shapes.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• The listener only accepts connections from the computer itself (127.0.0.1), which the tunnel uses, and only on a random path drawn for the run: any other request is refused.
  • The script deletes the subscription, disarms if it armed, and makes the Codespaces port private again at the end, even after an error or Ctrl+C.
  • If the script is killed before cleaning up, its subscription stays in place. Recent versions of hass-diagral then show a repair, webhook used by another installation, that lets you take the subscription back. With older versions, disabling then enabling the Diagral entry does the same.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Most calls are signed with an API key. When .env holds none and a scenario needs one, the script creates a temporary key at the start and deletes it at the end, even when a scenario fails or you press Ctrl+C.

To stop creating a key on every run, run once with --keep-apikey: the script prints two lines to paste into .env.

  DIAGRAL_API_KEY=…
  DIAGRAL_SECRET_KEY=…

The next runs use that key. The systems scenario shows how many keys each system has, which helps spot keys left behind.

docs.title: Diagnostics report
docs.text:
Every run that completes ends with a == diagnostics == section, in JSON:

  • unexpected_data: what Diagral sent that pydiagral's models did not expect, such as a missing field or an unknown value;
  • response_shapes: the structure of the last answer of each read, keys kept and values replaced.

Neither holds a value you typed nor an identifier: it is made to be shared as is, in a Diagnostics report issue. The report also gives pydiagral_version, and webhook_shapes after webhook-listen. When the output of a scenario looks wrong, or a warning asks you to report something, run that scenario and attach the report.

docs.title: Debug log
docs.text:
--debug logs every request and answer of pydiagral on the standard error. Keys, tokens, PIN codes and serial numbers are redacted, but the log still shows the names of your devices and groups: read it before posting it.

python try_pydiagral.py status --debug 2> debug.log

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Message Cause DIAGRAL_USERNAME and DIAGRAL_PASSWORD are required .env is missing, not next to the script, or does not set them DIAGRAL_SERIAL_ID is required for these scenarios Set it, or run systems to find it !! status failed: PIN code required to … Set DIAGRAL_PIN_CODE error: unknown scenario A typo in a scenario name: --help lists them Diagral request timed out Diagral did not answer within --timeout, 30 seconds by default. Its answers can be slow, which is why hass-diagral allows 60 seconds or more: run the scenario again with --timeout 60. The time printed after each scenario shows which ones are slow A webhook subscription already exists See One subscription per box Outside Codespaces, start a tunnel Start a tunnel and pass its address with --public-url The listener is not reachable In Codespaces, port 8080 is still private. Locally, the tunnel is not running, points to another port than --port, or a firewall blocks it: cloudflared needs to reach Cloudflare on port 7844 Cannot listen on port Another program uses the port: pick another with --port, and point the tunnel to it No notification arrived With --trigger arm, the exit delay may be longer than the listening time: raise --listen-for. Otherwise, run webhook to check that no other subscription took over

The script exits with code 0 when every scenario succeeded, 1 when one failed or the run stopped, and 2 on a wrong command line.
